what_sql_means.title: SQL is a language for working with stored data.
what_sql_means.bodyMarkdown:
Welcome to SQL Foundations. You do not need database experience before this course.

SQL stands for **Structured Query Language**. It is a language for working with information stored in a database.

[[image:sql_language_overview]]

People use SQL to answer questions such as:

- Which students are enrolled?
- Which products are low in stock?
- Which orders were placed today?

[[image:sql_question_to_data_flow]]

You will learn the query syntax step by step in the next module. For now, focus on the purpose:

> SQL lets you ask a database for the data you need.

[[image:sql_result_focus]]

what_a_database_is.title: A database keeps related information organized.
what_a_database_is.bodyMarkdown:
A **database** is an organized collection of data that a system can store, find, and update.

[[image:database_overview]]

A school might keep students, courses, and grades in one database. An online store might keep products, customers, and orders in another.

[[image:database_real_examples]]

Databases commonly organize information into **tables**. You will examine rows and columns closely in the next lesson.

[[image:database_contains_tables]]

The important idea here is simple:

> a database gives related information a structure that software can work with.

why_sql_is_useful.title: SQL connects a question to a result.
why_sql_is_useful.bodyMarkdown:
Stored data becomes useful when you can ask a clear question and get a clear answer.

[[image:data_everywhere]]

With SQL, analysts and developers can read, filter, sort, summarize, and later change stored data.

[[image:sql_actions_overview]]

The basic workflow is:

1. decide what you want to know;
2. write a query that asks for it;
3. run the query;
4. inspect the returned result.

[[image:ask_run_result_cycle]]

You do not need to memorize every SQL command at once. Each module will add one part of this workflow.

real_world_examples_of_databases.title: Different systems store different records.
real_world_examples_of_databases.bodyMarkdown:
Databases sit behind many systems you already use.

[[image:databases_in_daily_life]]

A school may track students and courses. A store may track products and orders. A media app may track users and playlists. A clinic may track patients and appointments.

[[image:school_database_example]]
[[image:store_database_example]]
[[image:media_database_example]]
[[image:hospital_database_example]]

The details change, but the pattern does not:

> the system stores organized records, and SQL helps people work with those records.

[[image:shared_database_pattern]]
